groups.high: Phishing sites can use HTTPS and valid TLS certificates. The padlock indicates an encrypted connection to the displayed domain, not that the business or message is trustworthy. Check the complete address before entering credentials, including spelling, unusual characters and the actual registered domain. google.com and g00gle.com are different names; a familiar brand in a subdomain or path does not establish ownership. A legitimate regional domain is not automatically a spoof merely because it differs from .com. Use a saved bookmark or type the organisation's known address instead of following an unexpected message. Contact the organisation through an independently verified channel if uncertain. Never bypass a browser certificate warning or download a certificate to satisfy an unsolicited instruction. Browsers normally perform hostname and certificate-chain checks; ordinary users do not need to analyse certificate transparency or entropy to identify every scam. No visual check guarantees safety, so use unique passwords and phishing-resistant multifactor authentication where available, and report suspicious messages.
groups.mid: A phishing site can have HTTPS and a valid certificate. The padlock means the link to that domain is protected by encryption. It does not prove the site or business is honest. Check the whole web address before entering a password. Look for spelling changes and unusual letters. google.com and g00gle.com are different names. A brand name in part of the address does not make it the real site. A real regional site is not fake just because it is not .com. Use a saved bookmark or type the known address. Do not click a surprise message. If unsure, find the real group another way. Use a number or site you found yourself. Never ignore a browser warning about a certificate. Do not install one because a message says to. Browsers check names and certificates in normal use. You do not need to study complex certificate logs for normal use. No check promises total safety. Use a different password for each account. Use phishing-resistant login where offered. Report suspicious messages.
groups.low: A scam site can have a padlock and HTTPS. This means the link to that domain is encrypted. It does not mean the people running it are honest. Check the full web address before you type a password. google.com is not g00gle.com. A brand name in part of an address does not prove it is real. A genuine regional site is not fake just because it is not .com. Use a saved bookmark or type the address you know. Do not use a link in a surprise message. If unsure, contact the group another way. Find the real number or site yourself. Do not ignore a certificate warning from the browser. Do not install a certificate because a message tells you to. The browser checks names and certificates in normal use. You do not need complex checks of certificate logs. No check stops every scam. Use a different password for each account and safer two-step login where offered. Report suspect messages.
groups.source_review: Checked FBI IC3 warning about valid HTTPS phishing sites; ordinary browser certificate checks distinguished from trust.
groups.notes: Removed false regional-domain spoof example, certificate SAN exactitude/entropy claims and HTTPS safety implication.

groups.high: A time-based one-time password (TOTP) is generated from a shared secret and a time counter using the algorithm in RFC 6238. Six digits and a 30-second step are common defaults, not universal requirements. The server may accept adjacent steps to allow clock drift or entry delay, so a code does not necessarily become unusable exactly 30 seconds after you see it. The verifier must reject reuse after successful validation to enforce one-time use. Short validity limits exposure but does not stop an attacker from relaying a phished code immediately. Never share a code with callers, supposed support staff or someone asking you to approve their login. Enter it only in the genuine service during a login you initiated. Keep the device clock accurate, protect the authenticator's secret and store recovery methods securely. If a code or secret was disclosed, secure the account and review active sessions. Prefer phishing-resistant methods such as passkeys or security keys when supported. TOTP adds protection beyond a password but is not immune to phishing.
groups.mid: A time-based one-time password, or TOTP, is a login code made from a shared secret and the time. RFC 6238 describes the system. Six digits and 30-second steps are common, not rules for every service. A server may allow a nearby time step for clock differences or typing delays. A code is not always rejected exactly 30 seconds after you see it. After a code is accepted once, the server must reject reuse. A short life helps, but a scammer can pass a stolen code to the real site right away. Never give a code to a caller or supposed support worker. Enter it only on the real service during a login you started. Keep your device clock right and protect the authenticator secret. Store recovery methods safely too. If you share a code or secret, secure the account and check active sessions. Passkeys or security keys resist phishing better where supported. TOTP adds protection, but cannot stop every phishing attack.
groups.low: TOTP is a time-based one-time password. It is a login code made from a secret and the time. RFC 6238 explains the system. A code often has six digits and changes every 30 seconds. Not all services use those settings. The server may allow nearby time steps if clocks differ or typing takes time. It may not reject a code exactly 30 seconds after you see it. Once accepted, a code must not be accepted again. A short life helps, but a thief can use a phished code at once. Do not share it with callers or supposed support staff. Type it only on the real site during a login you started. Keep your device clock correct. Guard the authenticator secret and keep recovery methods safe. If you disclose a code or secret, secure the account and check active sessions. Use passkeys or security keys where offered for better phishing resistance. TOTP helps, but is not phishing-proof.
groups.source_review: Checked RFC step recommendations, drift tolerance and replay rejection; NIST phishing resistance distinction.
groups.notes: Corrected algorithm, fixed-30-second mandate and contradictory previous-step rejection assertions.

groups.high: Public Wi-Fi deserves caution, but correctly validated HTTPS already encrypts traffic between an application or browser and the genuine bank. It is inaccurate to say every banking packet is readable merely because the Wi-Fi is public. Confirm the network with staff, avoid look-alike hotspots and do not bypass certificate warnings. For sensitive activity, a trusted cellular connection is a useful alternative. A reputable, correctly configured VPN can add an encrypted tunnel from the device to the VPN endpoint, reducing local-network visibility. It shifts some trust to the VPN provider and cannot make a phishing page, infected device or fraudulent transaction safe. Use the bank's genuine app or known HTTPS address, keep software updated, disable unnecessary sharing and automatic network joins, and use multifactor authentication. Log out and disconnect when finished. NIST SP 800-77 Revision 1 is Guide to IPsec VPNs, not Guidelines for Protecting Mobile Devices and Applications, and it does not establish the quoted universal AES-256 requirement for all public-Wi-Fi banking.
groups.mid: Public Wi-Fi needs care, but HTTPS already encrypts traffic between your device and the real bank. A public network does not make all banking data readable. Check the network name with staff and avoid look-alike hotspots. Never ignore a certificate warning. A trusted mobile-data connection is another option for sensitive tasks. A reputable VPN can add an encrypted link from your device to the VPN server. This reduces what the local network can see. It also means trusting the VPN provider. A VPN cannot make a fake bank site, infected phone or scam payment safe. Use the bank's real app or a known HTTPS address. Update software, turn off unneeded file sharing and automatic Wi-Fi joins, and use multifactor authentication. Log out and disconnect when done. NIST SP 800-77 Revision 1 is Guide to IPsec VPNs. It is not the mobile-device guide claimed here. It does not set one AES-256 rule for every person banking on public Wi-Fi.
groups.low: Take care on public Wi-Fi. HTTPS encrypts the link to the real bank. Being on public Wi-Fi does not make all bank data readable. Ask staff for the right network name. Avoid look-alike hotspots and never ignore a certificate warning. You can use trusted mobile data instead. A good VPN can add an encrypted link to its server. This hides more from the local network, but you must trust the VPN provider. It cannot make a fake bank site or infected device safe. It cannot stop you paying a scammer. Use the real bank app or type its known HTTPS address. Keep software up to date. Turn off file sharing and auto-join if not needed. Use two-step login too. Log out and disconnect when done. NIST SP 800-77 Revision 1 is Guide to IPsec VPNs, not a mobile-device guide. It does not require AES-256 for all public-Wi-Fi banking.
groups.source_review: Checked NIST public-Wi-Fi VPN/HTTPS advice and exact publication identity.
groups.notes: Corrected claim all public traffic plaintext, mandatory AES256, fake unsecured-network-name marker and VPN perfect security.

groups.high: When a service reports that a password was compromised, change it promptly on that service and every account reusing it. Attackers can automate attempts with stolen email–password pairs, a technique called credential stuffing. Reusing the password with a different username may also be risky. Use the genuine app or independently located site, not a reset link in an unexpected message. Set long, unique passwords, ideally generated and stored by a reputable password manager, and enable multifactor authentication or passkeys. Review recent activity, recovery details and active sessions; changing a password may not revoke existing sessions or stolen access tokens. Prioritise the email account because it can reset other accounts. If a notice exposes only an email address, that alone does not prove the password leaked, although phishing risk remains; follow the provider's confirmed guidance and act on evidence of compromise. NIST calls for action on compromised authenticators, not arbitrary universal password rotation as the only defence.
groups.mid: If a service says your password was compromised, change it there and anywhere you reused it. Thieves can test stolen email-and-password pairs on many sites. This is called credential stuffing. The same password may also be risky with another username. Open the real app or find the real site yourself. Do not trust a reset link in a surprise message. Use long, unique passwords for each account. A reputable password manager can make and store them. Add multifactor authentication or a passkey if offered. Check login history, recovery details and active sessions. A password change may not sign out someone who already has access. Secure your email account first because it can reset other logins. A leaked email address alone does not prove a password was stolen. It can still lead to phishing, so follow the service's verified advice. NIST says to act on compromised login methods. It does not say routine changes are the only way to stay safe.
groups.low: If a service says your password was stolen, change it there. Change it on every account that used it too. Thieves try stolen email-and-password pairs on many sites. This is credential stuffing. A reused password can be risky even with a different username. Go to the real app or site yourself. Do not follow a reset link in a surprise message. Make a long, unique password for each account. A trusted password manager can make and store them. Add a passkey or two-step login where offered. Check recent logins, recovery details and active sessions. Changing a password may not sign out someone already in the account. Start with email, since it can reset other accounts. A leaked email address alone does not prove the password leaked. But it can bring scam messages. Follow the provider's verified advice and act on signs of compromise. NIST calls for action on compromised logins. Regular password changes alone are not a complete defence.
groups.source_review: Checked NIST compromise-triggered action and strong unique credentials; session caveat retained.
groups.notes: Corrected reuse-versus-credential-stuffing definition, email-only equals password leak assumption and password-change-only defence.

groups.high: Apply least privilege to mobile apps: grant location or microphone access only when a feature genuinely needs it. Review background location separately from access while using the app, and use approximate rather than precise location where sufficient. On Android, open the app's permissions or the permission manager in Settings; labels and options vary by device and version. On iPhone, review Settings, Privacy & Security, Location Services and Microphone. Location choices may include Never or While Using the App; microphone access is typically an on/off permission, not a Never location setting. Deny unnecessary access for apps such as a basic calculator or flashlight. Calls, navigation, dictation or location alerts may lose relevant features if permission is removed, so check the purpose rather than disabling everything blindly. Review recent sensor activity and remove untrusted apps. Permissions are normally mediated by the operating system, not automatically granted broadly at installation. Restricting access reduces privacy risks but cannot guarantee protection against all tracking or a compromised operating system.
groups.mid: Give an app only the access it needs. Check background location and microphone permissions. An app may need location while open. It may not need it all the time. Use approximate location if precise location is not needed. On Android, open Settings. Find the app's permissions or the permission manager. Names vary by phone and version. On iPhone, open Settings, then Privacy & Security. Check Location Services and Microphone. Location may offer Never or While Using the App. Microphone access is usually a separate on/off switch. A basic calculator or flashlight should not need these sensors. Calls, maps, voice typing or location alerts may lose features. Check if they need the access before removing it. Check the purpose rather than turning everything off without thought. Review recent sensor use and remove apps you do not trust. The phone's system controls permissions. Apps do not normally get all access at install. Limiting access helps privacy. It does not stop all tracking or fix a compromised phone.
groups.low: Give apps only the access they need. Check the microphone and background location. Background location means an app can track where you are even when it is not open. A map may need location while open, not all the time. Approximate location may be enough. On Android, open Settings. Find the app's permissions or use the permission manager. Menus vary by phone and version. On iPhone, open Settings, then Privacy & Security. Check Location Services and Microphone. Location may have Never or While Using the App. The microphone has its own on/off switch. A simple calculator or flashlight should not need these sensors. Calls, maps, voice typing or alerts may lose features. Check what they need before you block access. Check why each app asks. Look at recent sensor use and remove untrusted apps. The phone's system controls permissions. Apps do not just get all access at install. Limits help cut risk. They cannot stop all tracking or fix a hacked phone.
groups.source_review: Checked Android and Apple permission controls; UI variability explicitly stated.
groups.notes: Corrected install-grants-all claim, wrong iOS microphone Never option and battery-settings bypass suggestion. Final claim-level spot review retained this practical qualification explicitly in Low.

groups.high: A hardware wallet can reduce exposure of cryptocurrency private keys by signing transactions inside a dedicated device rather than exporting keys to an internet-connected computer. Cold storage means keeping signing keys offline; not every hardware wallet is physically air-gapped. USB or Bluetooth connections are not air gaps, while some devices transfer unsigned and signed transactions through QR codes or removable media. Product architecture and limitations vary. Verify the recipient address, amount and network on the device's trusted display before approving. Malware can substitute transaction details, and phishing can still steal a recovery phrase or persuade the owner to authorise a harmful transaction. Buy through a trustworthy channel, verify setup and firmware, use a PIN and protect backups and any extra passphrase offline. Losing one phrase does not necessarily lose assets if usable keys or another backup remain; losing all access may be irreversible. NIST IR 8408 concerns stablecoin technology, not a universal cold-wallet endorsement. Offline storage reduces some risks but does not guarantee immunity from physical theft, supply-chain attacks or user error.
groups.mid: A hardware wallet signs a transaction inside a separate device. This can keep private keys safer. The private key is what authorises spending. Cold storage means keeping signing keys offline. Not every hardware wallet is air-gapped. USB and Bluetooth links are connections, not air gaps. Some devices exchange transaction data with QR codes or memory cards instead. Check the design of your actual product. Check the address, amount and network on the wallet's own trusted screen. Do this before you approve. Malware can change details on a computer. Phishing can still steal your recovery phrase or trick you into approving a harmful transfer. Buy from a trusted source and check setup and firmware. Use a PIN and keep backups and any extra passphrase safely offline. Losing a phrase does not always lose the assets if usable keys or another backup remain. Losing every way to access them may be irreversible. NIST IR 8408 is about stablecoins, not a general approval of cold wallets. Offline keys reduce some risks. They do not stop theft, tampering or every mistake.
groups.low: A hardware wallet signs a transaction in a separate device. This helps protect private keys from an online computer. Private keys authorise spending. Cold storage keeps signing keys offline. Not all hardware wallets are air-gapped. A USB or Bluetooth link is a connection, not an air gap. Some devices move transaction data with QR codes or memory cards. Check your product's design and limits. Before approving, check the address, amount and network on the wallet's own screen. Malware can change the computer's display. A phishing scam can steal a recovery phrase or trick you into approving a bad transfer. Buy from a trusted source and check setup and firmware. Use a PIN. Keep backups and any extra passphrase securely offline. Losing a phrase does not always lose the assets if another backup or usable keys remain. Losing all access may be permanent. NIST IR 8408 is about stablecoin technology. It is not a general endorsement of cold wallets. Offline storage reduces some risks. It cannot prevent physical theft, tampering or every mistake.
groups.source_review: Checked exact NIST report identity and manufacturer phishing/device-verification guidance. Architecture described conditionally across products.
groups.notes: Corrected air-gap/USB contradiction, zero key exposure guarantee, phishing immunity, universal MPC/HD/secure-element assumptions and source misattribution. Original Low FK exceeds Mid; overlapping acceptable ranges used where possible.

groups.high: Ransomware may encrypt systems, steal data or threaten publication to demand payment. The FBI discourages paying because payment does not guarantee recovery or deletion of stolen material and can finance further crime. The claimed Q4 2024 figure that 84% of paying victims failed to recover all data was not verified from the cited Coveware report and should not be repeated as evidence. If affected, isolate impacted systems from networks where safe, contact the organisation's incident-response team and preserve evidence. Follow expert advice before powering down or altering systems, since forensic evidence and ongoing harm must be considered. Report the incident to appropriate authorities, such as FBI IC3 or CISA in the United States. Restore from tested, clean backups only after containing the intrusion; a working decryptor does not prove the attacker is gone. Review notification duties, sanctions and other legal issues with qualified advisers. Maintain offline or immutable backups, updates, multifactor authentication and network segmentation. Payment is not a substitute for investigation, containment and recovery planning.
groups.mid: Ransomware may lock systems or steal data. Attackers may threaten to publish it unless they are paid. The FBI discourages payment because it does not guarantee recovery or deletion of stolen files. It can fund further crime. One claimed Q4 2024 figure says 84% of paying victims did not recover all data. This was not verified from Coveware. Do not use it as a confirmed fact. If attacked, safely isolate affected systems from the network. Contact the incident-response team. Keep evidence and seek expert advice before switching off or changing systems. Report the attack to the proper authorities, such as FBI IC3 or CISA in the US. Restore clean, tested backups only after the intrusion is contained. A tool that unlocks files does not prove the attacker has left. Ask qualified advisers about notice duties and legal issues, including sanctions. Prevention includes offline or immutable backups, software updates, multifactor authentication and network segmentation. Paying cannot replace investigation, containment and a recovery plan.
groups.low: Ransomware can lock files, steal them or threaten to make them public. Attackers ask for money. The FBI advises against paying. Payment does not guarantee your data comes back or that stolen copies are deleted. It can fund more crime. A claim says 84% of paying victims failed to get all data back in Q4 2024. That figure was not verified from Coveware. Do not treat it as fact. If attacked, safely disconnect affected systems from the network. Contact the team that deals with cyber attacks. Keep evidence. Get expert advice before switching systems off or changing them. Report to the right authority, such as FBI IC3 or CISA in the US. Use clean, tested backups after the attack is stopped from spreading. Unlocking files does not prove the attacker is gone. Ask experts about reporting duties, sanctions and other legal issues. Keep backups offline or protected from change. Use updates, two-step login and separate network zones. Payment is not a replacement for finding, stopping and recovering from the attack.
groups.source_review: Checked FBI no-payment/recovery guarantee guidance and CISA response principles. Claimed Coveware 84% statistic unverified, explicitly not endorsed.
groups.notes: Removed invented numerical recovery conclusion and distinguished encryption, exfiltration and recovery tasks.

groups.high: Third-party cookies can allow an embedded service, such as an advertising network, to recognise a browser across unrelated sites. The cookie belongs to the third-party domain; it is not simply copied from one visited site to another. Browser policies may block or partition these cookies, limiting cross-site use. Review privacy settings and enable suitable tracking protection. Deleting cookies can remove stored identifiers, but a weekly schedule is an optional habit, not a proven threshold that prevents tracking. Identifiers can be recreated, and websites can also use logins, fingerprinting and other storage. Private browsing does not guarantee anonymity. Clearing cookies may sign you out, remove preferences or disrupt site features. Consider blocking third-party cookies or using per-site exceptions only when necessary, and keep the browser updated. Cross-site tracking differs from theft of an authentication session cookie; a tracking identifier alone does not generally grant access to other accounts. Combine cookie controls with cautious sharing of personal data rather than assuming deletion erases an existing profile.
groups.mid: Third-party cookies can let an ad network recognise your browser on different sites. Other embedded services can use them too. The cookie belongs to that outside service. It is not simply copied from one site you visit to the next. Some browsers block or separate these cookies. This limits cross-site tracking. Check privacy settings and turn on suitable tracking protection. Deleting cookies removes some saved IDs. Doing it every week does not promise to stop tracking. New IDs can be set. Sites can also use account logins, fingerprinting and other storage. Private browsing does not make you anonymous. Clearing cookies may sign you out or remove saved settings. It may break a feature. You can block third-party cookies and allow a site exception only if needed. Keep the browser updated. A tracking cookie is not the same as a stolen login-session cookie. A tracking ID alone does not normally open your other accounts. Cookie controls help privacy. They do not erase a profile that a company already holds.
groups.low: A third-party cookie can let an outside service recognise your browser across sites. An ad network may use one. The cookie belongs to that service. It is not just copied from one site to the next. Some browsers block these cookies or keep them separate by site. Check the privacy settings and use tracking protection. Deleting cookies removes some stored IDs. Doing it weekly is a choice, not a guarantee that tracking stops. Sites can make new IDs. They can also use logins, fingerprinting or other storage to track you. Private browsing does not make you anonymous. Clearing cookies may sign you out or remove saved settings. Some features may stop working. Block third-party cookies if you can. Add a site exception only when needed. Keep the browser updated. Tracking is not the same as stealing a login-session cookie. A tracking ID does not normally unlock other accounts. Cookie controls help, but do not delete a profile a company already has.
groups.source_review: Checked browser-vendor cookie mechanics, partitioning and controls.
groups.notes: Removed false copied-cookie mechanics, cross-account-session-hijack claim and unsupported weekly entropy/economic tracking prevention guarantees.

groups.high: Separating Internet of Things devices, such as cameras, speakers and thermostats, from computers holding sensitive files can reduce lateral-movement risk. Use a properly configured guest or IoT network that blocks access to the main local network; a different Wi-Fi name alone does not prove isolation. Some routers provide this option directly, while managed networks may use VLANs plus firewall rules. VLAN separation by itself does not prohibit routed traffic, so verify the access policy. Allow only the specific management or discovery traffic needed; do not assume broad bidirectional access is required. Isolation may stop casting, printing or local control until suitable rules are configured. Keep devices and router firmware updated, change default passwords and disable unnecessary remote access or UPnP. Use client isolation and logs where appropriate. Segmentation reduces risk but does not guarantee containment or prevent an infected device from attacking internet hosts through an allowed connection. Follow the router manufacturer's instructions or obtain qualified assistance rather than copying generic firewall commands.
groups.mid: Put smart cameras, speakers and other IoT devices on a separate network from computers with private files. This can reduce the chance that one hacked device reaches the others. Use a guest or IoT network that blocks access to the main home network. A different Wi-Fi name alone does not prove it is separate. Some routers have a simple option. More complex setups may use VLANs and firewall rules. A VLAN separates traffic, but routing can still let it cross unless rules block it. Check the actual policy. Allow only the specific access needed for setup or control. Do not open broad two-way access by default. Casting, printing or local control may stop until safe exceptions are added. Update devices and router software, change default passwords and turn off unneeded remote access or UPnP. Use client isolation or logs if suitable. Separation reduces risk, but cannot stop every breach or prevent all attacks on internet hosts. Follow the maker's guide or ask an expert.
groups.low: Keep smart cameras, speakers and other IoT devices away from your main computers on the network. A guest or IoT network can help protect private files if it blocks access to the main network. A different Wi-Fi name is not proof of isolation. Some routers have a setting for this. Others use VLANs and firewall rules. A VLAN alone does not block traffic that a router allows across. Check the access rules. Allow only the links needed to manage devices. Do not open all two-way access. Casting, printing or local controls may need a limited exception to work. Update the devices and router. Change default passwords. Turn off remote access and UPnP if not needed. Use client isolation or logs where suitable. This helps limit harm from a hacked device. It is not a guarantee. A device may still attack internet systems through its allowed connection. Follow the router guide or ask for qualified help instead of copying general firewall commands.
groups.source_review: Checked CISA segmentation/guest-IoT network advice; routing and internet-egress limits qualified.
groups.notes: Corrected VLAN equals total containment and local isolation stops internet DDoS claims; avoided broad mandatory management access.

groups.high: Social engineering uses trust, fear, authority or urgency to persuade people to transfer money or reveal information. Treat unexpected payment requests and changes to bank details as unverified, even when they appear to come from a familiar account or voice. Email can be compromised and caller ID or audio can be spoofed. Pause and verify through an independently obtained channel, such as a known phone number from an existing record or the organisation's genuine site. Do not use a number, link or reply address supplied only in the suspicious message. For business payments, follow established approval controls and verify changes with the intended recipient. Independent verification is a process, not the same as a two-factor login code. Never share passwords, one-time codes or recovery phrases to prove identity. If money was sent, contact the bank or payment provider immediately to request recovery or freezing, preserve evidence and report promptly to relevant authorities, such as FBI IC3 in the United States. Verification reduces risk but does not prove every message is safe.
groups.mid: Social engineering means using trust, fear, authority or urgency to influence a person's choices. Verify a sudden payment demand or changed bank details. Do this even if it appears to come from someone familiar. Their email may be compromised. Caller ID or a voice can be faked. Pause before transferring money or sharing information. Contact the person or organisation through a channel you obtained independently. Use a known number in your records or on the genuine website. Do not use a number or link provided only in the suspicious message. Businesses should follow their payment-approval rules. Confirm bank-detail changes with the intended recipient. This independent check is not the same as a two-factor login code. Never disclose passwords, one-time codes or recovery phrases to prove identity. If payment was made, contact the bank or provider immediately about recovery or freezing. Preserve evidence and report promptly to the appropriate authorities, such as FBI IC3 in the US. Verification lowers risk. No single check guarantees safety.
groups.low: Scammers use trust, fear and urgency to make you act fast. Pause if a message asks for money or new bank details. It may look like it came from someone you know. Their email may be hacked. A caller ID or voice can be faked too. Check through a separate route you trust. Call a number you already know or find on the real website. Do not use the number or link from the suspect message. At work, follow payment-approval rules. Confirm new bank details with the real person who should be paid. This check is not a two-step login code. Never give passwords, one-time codes or recovery phrases as proof of who you are. If you sent money, call your bank or payment provider at once. Ask about stopping or recovering it. Keep the messages and other evidence. Report promptly to the right authority, such as FBI IC3 in the US. A check reduces risk, but no single check proves safety.
groups.source_review: Checked IC3 business email compromise prevention and rapid bank/reporting actions.
groups.notes: Clarified independent verification versus login MFA; removed invented trust-certainty claims.
